newsitem.title: PERU: Peru confirms misplaced tape caused air crash.
newsitem.headline: Peru confirms misplaced tape caused air crash.

text.p: Adhesive tape mistakenly left covering altitude and speed sensors caused the air crash in October of a Boeing 757 airliner that killed all 70 on board, Peru's Transport Ministry said late on Friday.

"According to the evidence that has been found, it has been concluded that staff cleaning the lower part of the aircraft did not remove protective adhesive tape when they finished their work and so the sensors remained obstructed," a report of a special commission set up by the Transport Ministry stated.
The report said the obstruction of these instruments explained the erroneous and confused information about height and speed received by the Boeing's pilots after takeoff.

The tape, covering sensors used to measure atmospheric pressure, was found in the plane's main body in the Pacific Ocean where it crashed on Oct. 2 soon after taking off for Santiago, Chile, from Lima in heavy fog.

Pilots from the airline, Aeroperu, that owned the plane, have rejected the tape theory claiming the Boeing would have crashed immediately on takeoff from Lima rather than half an hour later over the Pacific ocean.
The Transport Ministry added there was also pilot error in failing to follow the correct procedure once a warning light showed the plane was flying too low.

Despite the erroneous information received in the cockpit from the sensors, the pilot, Eric Schreiber, did not refer properly to readings from other instruments that could have helped him judge which information was wrong, the report added.

Immediately following the crash, the Peruvian government pinned the blame for the accident on technical faults that made the computers aboard the plane "go crazy," leaving Schreiber without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima.

"We've lost the basic instruments, both for height and for speed ... Where am I? Over land or sea?" Schreiber said during a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue with Lima air traffic control, before his jet plunged into the sea in the middle of the night.
The 70 dead came from Chile, Peru, Mexico, Ecuador, the United States, Italy, Great Britain, New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.

The accident, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa. The governemnt said it was likely that crash was due to the plane carrying too much cargo.
